I am Old Reed, the toad who teaches the tadpoles in our pond. We learn by doing, by listening, and by laughing until the moon tips sideways. Come close — no, closer — and let me tell you the story of the Night the Metal Herons Came, and how we kept the pond whole.

The machines arrived like a cold tide: tall heron-shaped things with brass knees and wings that clicked like stone on stone. They were not evil, just strange—made by distant hands and carrying a hunger for tidy lines where we like the messy curves of mud. Their first step sank a line of lilies. The water shook like a drum.

We could have waited for a single chief to shout orders. Instead, the croak-circle met in the shallow rim, and every voice counted. Little Sedge, who is only three tail-whorls old, had an idea: spool a curtain of spider-silk and breath into it. She croaked timidly; the elders leaned in. Old Mottle, who repairs broken shells and has a knack for pulley knots, added a twist. The fisherman-fireflies offered light; the reed-weavers supplied cordage. No single toad gave the plan; everyone folded their piece into it, like leaves layered to keep out rain.

We built strange machines of our own — not brittle steel, but clever devices grown with the pond’s patience. There were mud-gliders that slid under the herons’ brass talons, reed-gongs that sang with the push of a tadpole’s foot, and a great belly-net woven from cattail fluff and spider-thread that shaded the water like a second sky. Not one invention belonged to a single toad; each was signed with many croaks and many prints of slick bellies.

When battle came — and yes, there was bright and terrible fighting — we were not soldiers for a banner. We were neighbors who had traded favors for seasons. The watch-rotations we invented meant there was always a sentry who knew the lane of the willows, and the scavenger corps had maps etched in slug-slime to where the herons could be corralled. Old Hump, who once forgot to return a favor, led a band of drum-toads that beat patterns so precise the machines miscounted their steps and toppled into the mud like overfed cranes.

After the clangor, when the brass wings lay soggy and the herons hummed with the sound of defeat, we did not destroy the machines. We dismantled them carefully, learned from their ticks and springs, and used their parts to make pumps and lanterns. The herons were given places among us; the pond had room for both the old songs and the new gears.

Every tadpole who helped — even the ones who only fetched pebbles — is remembered by a ripple whenever our children leap. We taught the young to decide together: to speak, to listen, to fold new ideas into old songs. We taught them that strength comes from many small hands knowing which one to squeeze when the reed breaks.

So when you tell your tale, puff your throat and say it proudly: the pond is ours because we keep it together by talking, trading, and making strange machines when the moment asks for them. That is how we live. That is how we defend. That is how we make a place worth croaking about.
